agency: New York City Department of Correction (DOC)
title_code_or_exam: Civil service title Correction Officer; most recent open-competitive exam: Department of Citywide Administrative Services (DCAS) Exam No. 6303 (filing April 1 to May 29, 2026; testing expected to begin Aug. 13, 2026). Title code not confirmed from an official page.

hiring.summary: A candidate files for a city civil service exam run by the Department of Citywide Administrative Services, takes a computer-based multiple-choice test and is ranked on an eligible list. The Department of Correction's Applicant Investigation Unit then screens candidates through a background investigation, medical, psychological and agility tests and a drug screen before appointment to the Correction Academy. Appointment starts a 24-month probationary period, during which the officer must complete the academy and peace officer training.

nodes.title: Apply during the exam filing window
nodes.body: Candidates apply online through DCAS during a set filing period and pay a $68 fee, which can be waived for veterans, unemployed people and people receiving public assistance. Candidates must be at least 17 on the test date.
nodes.time: Filing window about 2 months (Exam 6303: April 1 to May 29, 2026)
nodes.who: Candidate; Department of Citywide Administrative Services
nodes.law: Civil Service Law §50(5) (exam fees); DCAS Notice of Examination No. 6303

nodes.title: Take the computer-based test
nodes.body: The multiple-choice test is given at a computer terminal. A score of 70% passes, and the score sets the candidate's rank.
nodes.time: Exam 6303 testing expected to begin Aug. 13, 2026, about 2.5 months after filing closed

nodes.title: Get ranked on the eligible list
nodes.body: Passing candidates are placed on an eligible list in score order and get a list number. State law says lists last one to four years; DCAS says this list is usually active for four years.
nodes.time: List lasts 1 to 4 years (usually 4); list reaches DOC about 4 to 6 months after the test, per an older DOC handout

nodes.title: Get called in list order
nodes.body: The city certifies names from the top of the list, and the department must choose among the three highest-ranked candidates willing to accept. DOC's Applicant Investigation Unit calls candidates to start screening.

nodes.title: Pass the background investigation
nodes.body: Investigators check documents and character, and candidates pay $75 for fingerprinting. People convicted of a felony or a domestic violence misdemeanor can't be appointed; a candidate disqualified on other grounds must get written reasons and a chance to explain.
nodes.time: 6 weeks to 6 months for screening, per an older DOC handout
nodes.law: Civil Service Law §50(4); DCAS Notice of Examination No. 6303

nodes.title: Pass the medical, psychological, agility and drug tests
nodes.body: Candidates take a medical exam, a written and oral psychological exam, a qualifying physical (agility) test and a drug screen. Each is a pass-fail gate before appointment.

nodes.title: Meet the requirements by appointment day
nodes.body: By the time of appointment a candidate must be 21, a U.S. citizen and a resident of New York City or Nassau, Westchester, Suffolk, Orange, Rockland or Putnam counties. The candidate also needs 39 college credits, or a high school diploma plus six months of qualifying experience such as military or law enforcement service, and at least a New York State learner's permit.
nodes.law: DCAS Notice of Examination No. 6303; Public Officers Law residency requirement (as stated in the notice)

nodes.title: Get appointed and train at the Correction Academy
nodes.body: Appointment is the first day of pay, and recruits go to the Correction Academy for training. Officers must be certified in state peace officer training within 12 months of appointment, and must get a New York State driver license before graduating.
nodes.time: About 4 months of academy, per DOC's 2024 handout (an older version said 5); peace officer certification within 12 months

nodes.title: Serve 24 months on probation
nodes.body: Probation lasts 24 months, and a recruit who fails the required training course is terminated. City rules add days on leave or limited duty to the probation period and allow up to six more months with the officer's written consent.
nodes.law: Civil Service Law §63; Personnel Rules and Regulations of the City of New York 5.2.1, 5.2.8

nodes.title: Permanent correction officer
nodes.body: An officer who completes probation holds a permanent competitive-class appointment and can be removed only for cause after written charges and a hearing.

end_to_end.text: DOC's 2024 Candidate Journey handout says a candidate can go from exam to correction officer in about 6 months, and adds that the process can vary by individual. An earlier, undated version of the handout said 12 to 17 months. Probation then runs another 24 months from appointment.

firing.summary: How a correction officer can be fired depends on whether they are still on probation. A probationary officer can be let go by notice without a hearing. A permanent officer is entitled to written charges, a trial before an administrative law judge at the city's Office of Administrative Trials and Hearings (OATH) and a final decision by the correction commissioner, which can be appealed to the city's Civil Service Commission or to state court. Under the Nunez federal consent decree, a court-appointed monitor tracks how long this process takes.

nodes.title: Misconduct is reported and investigated
nodes.body: DOC's Investigation Division looks into the allegation. For use-of-force cases, the Nunez consent judgment requires full investigations to finish within 120 days of referral, absent extenuating circumstances.
nodes.law: Nunez v. City of New York consent judgment §VII ¶9

nodes.question: Is the officer still on probation?

nodes.title: Commissioner ends employment by notice
nodes.body: After at least two months of probationary service, the agency head can terminate a probationer whose conduct or performance is unsatisfactory by notice to the officer and to DCAS. A probationer who fails the required training course can also be terminated. City rules require no hearing.
nodes.time: Any time after 2 months and before probation ends
nodes.law: Personnel Rules and Regulations of the City of New York 5.2.7

nodes.title: Terminated without a hearing
nodes.body: Under settled New York case law, a probationer has no right to a hearing and can challenge the firing in court only by showing bad faith or an improper or illegal reason.

nodes.title: Trials Division serves written charges
nodes.body: The officer gets written charges and at least eight days to answer in writing. Charges must be brought within 18 months of the misconduct unless it would be a crime. In use-of-force cases, the Trials Division must make best efforts to serve charges within 30 days of the investigators' recommendation.
nodes.time: Within 18 months of the incident (unless a crime); at least 8 days to answer
nodes.law: Civil Service Law §75(2), §75(4); Nunez consent judgment §VIII ¶3(c)

nodes.title: Possible suspension pending the hearing
nodes.body: The officer can be suspended without pay while charges are pending, but for no more than 30 days. If acquitted, the officer gets back pay for the suspension, less any unemployment benefits.

nodes.title: Pre-trial conference at OATH
nodes.body: The case is filed with OATH and a judge holds a pre-trial conference aimed at settlement. Most formal discipline cases end in a negotiated plea agreement: 73% in the period covered by the monitor's January 2026 report.
nodes.time: No statutory clock; Nunez expedited cases: conference scheduled within 20 business days of the investigation closing
nodes.who: DOC Trials Division; officer and union counsel; OATH judge

nodes.title: Trial before an OATH judge
nodes.body: If the case doesn't settle, an OATH administrative law judge holds a trial, where DOC has the burden of proof. The judge then sends a report and recommendation on facts and penalty to the commissioner.
nodes.time: Use-of-force trials now scheduled within 50 days of the pre-trial conference; reports due within 45 days of the last trial day (OATH practice described by the monitor)
nodes.who: OATH administrative law judge; DOC Trials Division; officer

nodes.title: Commissioner decides guilt and penalty
nodes.body: The correction commissioner makes the final decision. Penalties range from a reprimand, a fine of up to $100 or unpaid suspension of up to two months to demotion or dismissal.
nodes.time: No general clock found; Nunez expedited cases: within 15 business days of the report

nodes.title: Officer chooses one appeal route
nodes.body: The officer can appeal to the New York City Civil Service Commission within 20 days, and that decision is final. Or the officer can sue in state Supreme Court under Civil Practice Law and Rules Article 78, which allows four months.
nodes.time: 20 days (Civil Service Commission, plus 3 if served by registered mail) or 4 months (Article 78)
nodes.who: Officer; New York City Civil Service Commission or state Supreme Court
nodes.law: Civil Service Law §76(1), §76(3); Civil Practice Law and Rules §217(1)

nodes.title: Dismissal stands or is changed
nodes.body: The union contract's grievance and arbitration process excludes disciplinary matters, so discipline goes through this statutory path rather than arbitration. Separately, a felony conviction automatically vacates a public office under state law.

stats.text: In the monitoring period covered by the Nunez monitor's Jan. 13, 2026 report (tables run through June 2025), DOC's Trials Division resolved 269 formal discipline cases: 73% by negotiated plea agreement and two by OATH trial.
272 cases were pending with the Trials Division at the end of that period, compared with more than 1,000 at the end of each monitoring period from 2020 to 2022.
67% of the cases closed in that period involved incidents that happened more than a year earlier.
The monitor says that even under ideal conditions a formal discipline case takes at least 180 days to fully resolve.
OATH held six use-of-force trials in 2024, averaging 117 days from pre-trial conference to report and recommendation, compared with 26 trials averaging 320 days in 2021.

caveats: The exam notice for Exam No. 6303 (amended April 29, 2026) is treated as the controlling statement of candidate requirements. Two older DOC documents differ: the Join the Boldest FAQ says the minimum age to test is 17 1/2 (the notice says 17), and an undated DOC handout requires a full driver license and 60 college credits at appointment (the notice requires a learner's permit and 39 credits, with the academy adding 21). Sources 51 and 52 are kept only to document the discrepancy.

Hiring durations come from two DOC 'Candidate Journey' handouts: the 2024 version says about 6 months with a four-month academy, and an older undated version says 12 to 17 months with a five-month academy. Both say timing varies by individual. No statute sets these clocks.

The 24-month probation comes from the exam notice. Personnel Rule 5.2.1 sets a one-year default 'unless otherwise set forth in the terms and conditions of the certification.' I did not find the specific DCAS determination that sets 24 months for this title.

The Nunez Action Plan's expedited timelines (investigation within 30 business days, referral and pre-trial conference within 20, OATH adjudication within 35, commissioner's decision within 15) apply only to cases identified for expedited handling: conduct that would merit termination and egregious conduct risking serious harm. They are not general deadlines. The 120-day investigation and 30-day charge-service standards come from the consent judgment's use-of-force provisions and apply to use-of-force cases.

The 50-day trial scheduling and 45-day report deadlines are OATH practices for use-of-force cases as described by the Nunez monitor, not published rules I verified. The monitor says the 50-day standard took effect after COBA's Article 78 challenge was dismissed.

The union contract language comes from the 2011-2019 executed contract, the most recent full contract text I found. The 2022-2027 COBA unit agreement on the Office of Labor Relations site is a three-page PDF; only its last page has extractable text, the rest appears to be scanned images, and no OCR tool was available. I can't confirm whether the 2022-2027 agreement changed Article XXI, but its readable page says it resolves unit bargaining matters under the uniformed coalition memorandum of agreement.

Article XXI of the 2011-2019 contract excludes 'disciplinary matters' from the grievance definition in its subsection on agency rules, 'except as otherwise provided in this Section 1a.' I found no provision offering arbitration of Civil Service Law §75 discipline as an alternative.

The 2011-2019 contract provides health coverage when a suspension without pay before trial runs past 30 days, which suggests longer suspensions occur in practice even though Civil Service Law §75(3) caps unpaid suspension at 30 days. I did not verify the legal basis for suspensions longer than 30 days (for example, delays requested by the employee).

Criminal Procedure Law §2.10(25) covers correction officers 'of any penal correctional institution' and does not name the city Department of Correction explicitly. The exam notice separately requires officers to meet state peace-officer requirements.

The Swinton v. Safir quote is from a vLex copy of the Court of Appeals decision because Justia and CourtListener did not return text. It is cited only for the settled rule that probationers can be dismissed without a hearing absent bad faith.
The stats come from the Nunez monitor's report filed Jan. 13, 2026, whose discipline tables cover through June 2025. They are the monitor's figures and I did not independently check them.
